title: Worlds beyond worlds
hookLine: there are worlds beneath worlds and skies above skies, beyond counting (Japji 22)
tomorrow: how do you make a coin out of a life?

cards: Phone lights held up at a concert, thousands of them in the dark, and for a second the crowd looks like a sky.
The janamsakhis tell of an evening at the temple of Jagannath in Puri, at the hour of aarti, when lamps are waved on a platter.

Guru Nanak, they say, looked up and sang of the aarti already happening overhead: the sky is the platter, the sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls, the scented breeze the incense, and all the forests flowers.

teach.b: That's the size of sky Guru Nanak sang in, and the Japji's twenty-second stanza pushes it further. Underworlds below underworlds, it says, and a hundred thousand skies above skies.
Searchers went to the very edges and grew weary, and the Vedas say so. Other scriptures speak of eighteen thousand worlds, and of one essence behind them.
If it could be counted, it would be written down; but the counting runs out first.
Nanak says: call Him great; He alone knows Himself. So, in the Japji, creation is beyond counting, and so is the Creator, and the fitting answer to that size is praise, not a number.
A neighbor tradition looks up at the same sky. Psalm 147 says of God: "He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names." Both look up, and both end in praise.
The psalm pictures every star numbered and named by God.
The Japji says any count, ours or the books', gives out, and only He knows Himself. One holds the count in God's hands; the other says no written count can hold it.
And so, in the story, Guru Nanak's aarti has the whole sky for its lamps.

how: Sikhs recite the Japji each morning; Guru Nanak's sky-aarti hymn, 'gagan mai thaal', is sung in the Sikh evening prayers and in kirtan.

o: more worlds and skies than anyone can count
seven heavens, each ruled by its own god
the other planets that science has mapped

games.q: worlds beyond worlds: tap the pairs.
p: he telleth the number of the stars

s: the Japji gives a final count of the worlds
the counting runs out, it says; only He knows Himself.
Psalm 147 and the Japji both answer the sky with praise
both look up and praise; they differ on whether the count can be held.
Guru Nanak's sky hymn is a list of the planets
it's an aarti: the sky the platter, sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls.

games.q: a friend who loves the Psalms says Psalm 147 and the Japji say exactly the same thing. what's the fair answer?
o: both look up and praise, but the psalm has God number the stars; the Japji says the count runs out.
they're identical; every scripture teaches exactly one thing about the sky.
they disagree completely, so one of them has to be wrong about God.
games.why: shared: the sky leads to praise. different: every star numbered and named, or beyond any count at all.

practice: If you can, step outside or go to a window, and walk a few slow steps while looking up. Find the farthest thing you can see, a star, a cloud, a plane's light, and keep your eyes on it as you walk.
Let the sky be bigger than the list in your head.

wordCard.voice: Worlds beyond worlds: the Japji's twenty-second stanza, skies above skies, more than any count can hold.

orig.note: Gurmukhi, Japji stanza 22: underworlds below underworlds, a hundred thousand skies above skies.

carryVoice: Here's the line: beyond counting, so praise instead of a number. Three of five from the Japji.

sources.ref: Japji, stanza (pauri) 22, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 5 (underworlds below underworlds, a hundred thousand skies above skies; seekers grew weary, the Vedas say; the Kateb speak of eighteen thousand worlds, one essence; if it could be written it would be, but the account perishes; call Him great, He alone knows Himself)

Guru Nanak, Raag Dhanasari, 'gagan mai thaal', Guru Granth Sahib Ang 13 (the sky the platter, sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls, the breeze the incense, the forests flowers); janamsakhi setting at Jagannath Puri
